statement: A grid of square cells has $7$ rows and $9$ columns. What is the least positive integer $n$ such that every choice of $n$ different cells of the grid must include two cells that touch, either along a side or at a corner?

choices.misconception: I covered only the 12 full 2 by 2 blocks in the first 6 rows and the first 8 columns, forgot the last row and the last column, and answered 12 + 1.
I forgot the seventh row, so I used 3 rows of blocks and 5 columns of blocks, 15 boxes in all, and answered 15 + 1.
I forgot the ninth column, so I used 4 rows of blocks and 4 columns of blocks, 16 boxes in all, and answered 16 + 1.
I found the 20 cells in the odd rows and odd columns, no two of which touch, and gave that size instead of one more than it.

hints: Any two cells inside the same $2 \times 2$ block touch.

This is pigeonhole: cut the grid into as few pieces as possible so that any two cells in the same piece touch. Then show you cannot do better by finding a set of cells, one in each piece, with no two touching.
Group the rows as $1$-$2$, $3$-$4$, $5$-$6$, $7$ and the columns as $1$-$2$, $3$-$4$, $5$-$6$, $7$-$8$, $9$. That makes $4 \cdot 5 = 20$ pieces, each at most $2 \times 2$.

solutions.reliable: Group the rows into $\{1,2\}, \{3,4\}, \{5,6\}, \{7\}$ and the columns into $\{1,2\}, \{3,4\}, \{5,6\}, \{7,8\}, \{9\}$. Each row group and column group together cut out a piece of at most $2 \times 2$ cells, giving $4 \cdot 5 = 20$ pieces, and any two cells in the same piece touch. So any $21$ cells put two in the same piece, and those two touch. On the other hand, the $20$ cells in rows $1, 3, 5, 7$ and columns $1, 3, 5, 7, 9$ are pairwise at least $2$ apart in their row or their column, so no two of them touch. Hence $20$ cells do not force a touching pair and $21$ do: $n = 21$. The transferable idea: a pigeonhole answer needs two halves, boxes that force the property and an example showing one fewer is not enough.
solutions.elegant: Give each chosen cell the $2 \times 2$ square that has it as its top-left cell, after adding one blank row below the grid and one blank column to its right. If two of these squares overlapped, their top-left cells would differ by at most $1$ in row and in column, so they would touch. So for a choice with no two cells touching, the squares do not overlap and all fit inside an $8 \times 10$ rectangle of area $80$, which allows at most $80 / 4 = 20$ cells. The $20$ cells in odd rows and odd columns show that $20$ is possible, so the answer is $21$.
